title: 2024 budget direction and Fischer-Hallman left-turn access
subtitle: Employment lands strategy, speed cameras, Route 34 extension, expropriations, countryside line deferral, equity resolution and auditor appointment
overview: Regional Council set the direction for the 2024 budget. It approved a review timetable and guiding principles, and directed staff to aim for a 2024 tax rate impact of 6% to 8% for direct regional services, excluding police. Staff will also set out service expansions, service reductions, capital delays and reserve draws that would be needed to reach that range.

Council approved a left-in turn at a new commercial access on Fischer-Hallman Road {{vote:m15}}, against staff advice. The access can be reduced to right-in, right-out if turning demand or safety problems arise. Council also funded an employment lands shovel-ready strategy and approved expanding automated speed enforcement to all school zones by the end of 2028, subject to budget approval. A Route 34 transit extension starts September 5, 2023.

Other decisions included expropriations for the Farmers Market Trail and a roundabout at Cedar Creek and Trussler roads, a one-year appointment of KPMG as external auditor, and a deferral of a Lobbyist Registry to the 2024 budget. A motion on the countryside line was deferred to August so council can hear legal advice. After a closed session, council approved a land purchase and a land-exchange agreement with the City of Waterloo.

decisions.item: 2024 Plan and Budget process and principles
decisions.detail: Council approved the 2024 budget review timetable and a set of guiding principles, adding items on non-mandatory services, employment lands, staff reductions and equity.

Staff were directed to develop the 2024 budget for a 6% to 8% tax rate impact for direct regional services excluding police, and to outline expansions, reductions, capital delays and reserve use needed to reach it.

Council approved a controlled access amendment allowing right-in, right-out and left-in movements, with the left-in removable if peak demand reaches 120 movements per hour or safety and delay problems arise.
Council started the strategy before the 2024 budget by extending the Dillon Consulting contract and engaging Newmark for a market-readiness review.

Council approved expropriations for the Farmers Market Trail and Cedar Creek and Trussler intersection, expanded automated speed enforcement to all school zones by 2028 subject to 2024 budget approval, and extended Route 34 from September 5, 2023.

Council approved $340,000 in major arts and culture grants, a new housing fee-for-service protocol, and a resolution asking the CAO to consider embedding anti-racism, equity and reconciliation in Regional operations.
KPMG LLP was appointed external auditor for the 2023 fiscal year at $172,400 plus taxes.
Council deferred a motion to reaffirm no new residential areas in the countryside line and explore removing 70 hectares from the urban area until August 2023.

debate: On Fischer-Hallman, staff said a left-in would mean drivers crossing two lanes and then a multi-use trail beside a bus stop, creating conflict points, and that the site already has other accesses. Staff said the road's roundabout design has been planned since 2015.

The developer's delegates said the grocery tenant requires the left-in, and that traffic studies found 50 metres of turn storage adequate. They proposed signage and tighter curb radii to reduce trail conflicts, and said they would accept a condition removing the turn if volumes grew.

Supporters of the left-in said it matched earlier council decisions on similar sites and supports 15-minute neighbourhoods. Opponents raised pedestrian and cyclist safety, idling traffic, and the access already available. One councillor with low vision said a left turn felt unsafe.

On the budget, councillors asked for a clear view of which reductions are low-impact and which affect services. One councillor warned against treating staff as the place to cut, and another said a 6% target would show residents the consequences of a lower increase.

On employment lands, a business delegate urged council not to defer, citing a very low industrial vacancy rate and missed opportunities. One councillor said climate and natural environment were not mentioned in the presentations. On the countryside line motion, staff said the Minister's decision cannot be appealed and changes could invite legal challenge.
